quests.instruction: A new electric metro line opens and many drivers switch to it. What might happen to the air on nearby streets?
quests.hint: Fewer fumes in the air.
quests.explanation: Fewer cars on the road means fewer exhaust fumes. Electric trains make no exhaust where they run, so the air can get cleaner.
quests.funFact: Cities that invest in metro lines often see less traffic on main roads.

quests.instruction: Fuel prices are very high. Which mix of travel helps a city keep people moving?
quests.hint: Think low-cost, shared, and people-powered.
quests.explanation: Buses carry many people for little fuel, and bicycles and walking use none. Together they keep a city moving even when fuel is costly.
quests.funFact: Cities that mix transport options are often easier to travel in.

quests.instruction: A bus company adds more buses and gives them their own lanes. What is likely to happen to the number of passengers over time?
quests.hint: Better service attracts more riders.
quests.explanation: Buses that arrive often and avoid jams are more useful, so more people choose them. The line on a chart goes up.
quests.funFact: Reliable services build trust, and trust brings passengers.

quests.instruction: Which pair of actions makes crossing a busy road safest?
quests.hint: Pause first, then use your eyes.
quests.explanation: Stopping at the kerb and looking carefully lets you check the traffic before you step out. Rushing, headphones, or phones can make you miss danger.
quests.funFact: Looking and listening together gives you the most information.

quests.instruction: A friend wants to send a message while cycling. What is the best advice?
quests.hint: A rider needs both hands and both eyes.
quests.explanation: A moment of looking at a phone can mean riding blind. Waiting until you stop keeps you and others safe.
quests.funFact: Many countries ban hand-held phone use while driving, and it is just as risky when riding.

quests.instruction: Which road user is least protected and needs the most care from others?
quests.hint: No frame, no helmet, only feet.
quests.explanation: A walker has no vehicle around them to absorb a crash. Drivers must slow down near pedestrians, and walkers must take care too.
quests.funFact: Many road safety rules are made first to protect people on foot.

quests.instruction: On a short trip, which makes the most pollution for each person carried: a car with one person, a full bus, or a bicycle?
quests.hint: Compare how many people share each vehicle's pollution.
quests.explanation: A car with one passenger makes fumes for just one person. A full bus shares them among many people, and a bicycle makes none.
quests.funFact: A car carrying only one person is one of the least efficient ways to move people.

quests.instruction: Which saves the most fuel per person: a car with one driver, or a car full of passengers?
quests.hint: Sharing the journey shares the fuel.
quests.explanation: A car uses about the same fuel whether it holds one person or four. Sharing the ride means each person uses less.
quests.funFact: Some roads have carpool lanes for cars with several passengers.

quests.instruction: Hydrogen, biogas, and electricity are all alternatives to burning what in vehicles?
quests.hint: It is pumped from underground and made into petrol and diesel.
quests.explanation: Oil is a fossil fuel that will run out and pollutes when burned. Cleaner alternatives help reduce the pollution from transport.
quests.funFact: Many vehicle makers now offer electric versions of their models.

quests.instruction: Which set of features makes a station easier for everyone to use?
quests.hint: Think step-free, clear, and easy to hear.
quests.explanation: Lifts remove steps, clear signs help people find their way, and announcements help people who cannot see screens. Together they welcome everyone.
quests.funFact: Features designed for disabled travellers often make travel easier for everyone.

quests.instruction: Who benefits from a ramp at a station?
quests.hint: Think of anyone with wheels.
quests.explanation: Ramps help wheelchair users, parents with prams, and people with wheeled luggage. Many people benefit from step-free routes.
quests.funFact: This is sometimes called the kerb-cut effect, because features made for some people help many.

quests.instruction: Good designers ask disabled travellers what they need before planning a station. Which symbol means asking questions?
quests.hint: It is a curly line with a dot.
quests.explanation: Asking is the best way to learn what people need. Travellers know their own needs better than anyone.
quests.funFact: Listening to users is a big part of good design.

quests.instruction: A town counts 1,200 trips in a day: 600 by car, 300 by bus, 200 on foot, and 100 by bicycle. Which type makes up one quarter of the trips?
quests.hint: A quarter of 1,200 is 300.
quests.explanation: 1,200 divided by 4 is 300. The bus has 300 trips, which is a quarter.
quests.funFact: Fractions help planners compare how people travel.

quests.instruction: In the same count, how many trips are not made by car?
quests.hint: Add the bus, walking, and cycling trips.
quests.explanation: 300 plus 200 plus 100 is 600, so half of all trips are not by car.
quests.funFact: Counting trips helps towns plan buses and paths.

quests.instruction: The town wants at least two-thirds of all trips to be without a car. In the same count, has it reached this goal?
quests.hint: Work out 1,200 divided by 3, then double it.
quests.explanation: Two-thirds of 1,200 is 800 trips, but only 600 are not by car. So the goal is not yet reached.
quests.funFact: Goals help towns measure progress over time.

quests.instruction: After a flood, a town needs 2 tonnes of supplies. A helicopter can carry 500 kilograms per trip. How many trips are needed?
quests.hint: 2 tonnes is 2,000 kilograms.
quests.explanation: 2,000 divided by 500 is 4, so the helicopter needs four trips.
quests.funFact: Relief teams plan loads carefully so nothing is wasted.

quests.instruction: After an earthquake, rubble blocks a road. Which strong vehicle can push and clear it?
quests.hint: It is heavy and made for moving earth and stones.
quests.explanation: Heavy vehicles like tractors and bulldozers can clear rubble so that other vehicles can pass. They are among the first to arrive after a disaster.
quests.funFact: Clearing roads quickly lets rescue teams and supplies get in.

quests.instruction: A rescue helicopter searches for a missing hiker at night. Which tool helps it find them?
quests.hint: It gives a bright beam.
quests.explanation: Helicopters carry powerful searchlights, and often heat-sensing cameras. They help crews spot people in the dark.
quests.funFact: Search teams also use thermal cameras to see body heat.

quests.instruction: Which animal was nicknamed the 'ship of the desert' because it carried travellers across the sand?
quests.hint: It has a hump.
quests.explanation: Camels travel long distances in hot, dry places, so they carried goods and people across deserts for centuries.
quests.funFact: Caravans of camels crossed deserts along ancient trade routes.

quests.instruction: In old stories, steam locomotives were nicknamed the 'iron horse'. Which vehicle is that?
quests.hint: It runs on rails and blows out steam.
quests.explanation: Steam locomotives replaced horses for pulling heavy loads over long distances. People called them iron horses.
quests.funFact: The nickname iron horse was widely used when railways first spread across continents.

quests.instruction: In London, the underground railway has a famous nickname, 'the Tube'. Which vehicle is that?
quests.hint: It runs in tunnels below the streets.
quests.explanation: Its round tunnels look like tubes, which is how the nickname came about.
quests.funFact: Parts of the Tube run above ground, and many stations are open to the sky.

quests.instruction: It runs on rails along the street, gets power from overhead wires, and is quieter and cleaner than a diesel bus. What is it?
quests.hint: Look for rails in the street and wires above.
quests.explanation: Trams are electric, so they make no exhaust where they run. They carry many passengers on city streets.
quests.funFact: Some tram systems have been running for well over a century.

quests.instruction: It floats, makes short trips back and forth all day, and lets people and cars drive on and off. What is it?
quests.hint: It is like a floating bridge.
quests.explanation: A ferry shuttles back and forth across short stretches of water. Cars and people board at ramps.
quests.funFact: Some ferries run all day, and some run through the night.

quests.instruction: It has four wheels, runs on a battery, makes no exhaust, and plugs in to charge. What is it?
quests.hint: It is a small private road vehicle.
quests.explanation: An electric car stores power in a battery and uses an electric motor. It makes no exhaust from a tailpipe.
quests.funFact: Electric cars can be charged at home, at work, or at public charging points.

quests.instruction: You are running late for school. The crossing shows a red person, and no cars are in sight. What should you do?
quests.hint: Safety is worth a few seconds.
quests.explanation: Wait for the green person. A vehicle may be coming faster than you think, and the signal is there to keep you safe.
quests.funFact: Crossing signals are timed so that traffic and walkers take turns.

quests.instruction: Someone tosses a drinks can onto the road from a car window. Where should litter go?
quests.hint: Think of the container with a lid or an open top, placed along streets and in stations.
quests.explanation: Litter on roads can harm animals, block drains, and cause accidents. Always put it in a bin.
quests.funFact: Many places have fines for dropping litter on roads.

quests.instruction: A pavement has a big crack that could trip walkers. Which helper can repair it once it is reported?
quests.hint: They work on roads and paths.
quests.explanation: Construction workers repair roads and paths. Reporting hazards to the right people helps keep everyone safe.
quests.funFact: Many councils have phone numbers or apps for reporting broken pavements.

quests.instruction: A group of ten, including two wheelchair users, travels 100 kilometres to the coast. Which choice is accessible, comfortable, fairly cheap, and fairly clean?
quests.hint: Think about spaces for wheelchairs, seats, and electricity.
quests.explanation: Trains have step-free access, spaces for wheelchairs, and comfortable seats, and many are electric. Planes and helicopters cost much more and make more pollution.
quests.funFact: Many trains have special spaces for wheelchair users and prams.

quests.instruction: A city wants cleaner air, safer streets, and quicker journeys for everyone. Which set of ideas helps most?
quests.hint: Think clean, shared, and safe.
quests.explanation: Electric buses cut fumes, and protected cycle lanes make streets safer. Together they let more people travel in less space.
quests.funFact: Many cities are adding both electric buses and cycle lanes.

quests.instruction: Good transport helps people reach school, work, health care, friends, and fun. What is its main job?
quests.hint: It brings people together.
quests.explanation: Transport links people with the places and people they need. A good system is safe, fair, clean, and works for everyone.
quests.funFact: People have been inventing better ways to travel for thousands of years.
